newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate confirms Barshefsky as trade chief.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate confirms Barshefsky as trade chief.

text.p: The Senate confirmed Charlene Barshefsky as U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday after voting to lift a barrier to her taking office.
The votes were near unanimous, reflecting wide admiration for Barshefsky's skills as a tough trade negotiator.

President Bill Clinton named Barshefsky to succeed Mickey Kantor, who moved to head the Commerce Department last April. She was Kantor's deputy for three years and has been serving as acting trade representative since his departure.

Before confirming Barshefsky on a 99-1 vote, the Senate approved a waiver of a 1995 law that bars anyone who previously represented a foreign government in a trade dispute with the United States from occupying the top trade post.

The waiver was needed because Barshefsky represented the Canadian lumber industry in a dispute with the United States while she was with a Washington law firm. It was approved 98-2 and sent to the House for action.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott voted against waiving the law and Colorado Republican Wayne Allard voted against both the waiver and confirmation.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat, told the Senate he had received a letter from President Clinton's legal counsel Charles Ruff saying that "to ensure the absolute propriety" of Barshefsky's appointment she would not take her post until the waiver resolution had been enacted into law.
Senators of both parties lavished praise on Barshefsky, 46, who has gone to the brink of trade wars with Japan and China to secure agreements.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, told the Senate Barshefksy had been a vigorous advocate and defender of U.S. trade interests and had showed toughness and resolve.
He noted that the new trade representative would have to deal with difficult trade issues, including the increasingly complicated trade relationship with China.
Barshefsky holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Wisconsin and a law degree from Catholic University in Washington. She lives in Washington with her husband and two daughters.
